To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

extranodal lymphomas are often difficult to diagnose because they are frequently asymptomatic, may occur in sites other than lymphoid tissue, and may mimic benign lymphoid proliferations histologically.

extranodal noncutaneous (ENNC) lymphoid neoplastic lesions that meet the histopathologic criteria for benign lymphoproliferative lesions frequently contain clonally expanded B-cell populations and that the clonal B-cell populations in ENNC lymphoproliferations represent a spectrum of disease ranging from benign lymphoid hyperlasias to low-grade lymphoma and that the spectrum of disease is continuous.

We investigated 16 lymphoproliferative lesions occurring in the ocualr adnexa, breast, salivary gland and thyroid gland and meeting the histopathological and immunophenotypical criteria of benign lympho-proliferation for the presence of monoclonal and polyclonal B-cell populations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new approach to the study of the development of a continuous and progressive spectra of B-cell neoplasm.
the development of a new class of lymphomas, which are not necessarily identical.
the molecular genetics and immunophenotype of extranodal lymphoid neoplastic proliferations occurring in sites that have been previously considered as benign lymphoid hyperlasias.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the lymphoid hyperplastic lesions are neoplastic and that they should be treated with a low dose of radiation therapy.
the majority of these extranodal, benign-appearing lymphoid proliferations are not benign, but rather are malignant lymphomas in an early stage of development.
extranodal noncutaneous B-cell lymphoid hyperplastic neoplasms represent a continuous spectrum, with the potential for progression to malignant lymphoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
extranodal B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders (BCLP) are a spectrum of B-cell lymphoplasia that includes benign lymphoid hyperlasias and malignant lymphomas.
extranodal B-cell lymphoid neoplastic disorders are more common in patients with AIDS, in the elderly, and in the setting of other lymphoproliferative disorders.

the majority of lymphoid proliferations in the ocular-adnexal, breast and salivary-gland regions, and the thyroid gland, which satisfy the histopathologic criteria for benign lymphoproliferative disease, are clonal and therefore neoplastic.
The main takeaway from our work is that

extranodal lymphoid proliferations meeting the histopathological and immunophenotypical criteria of benign lymphoproliferation may represent a continuum of B cell neoplasia ranging from low grade lymphoma to malignant lymphoma.
the majority of extranodal noncutaneous benign lymphoid hyperlasias are actually low-grade B-cell lymphomas, and the distinction between the two entities is often arbitrary.

extranodal lymphoid neoplastic lesions, including those meeting the histopathological and immunophenotypical criteria for benign lymphoproliferations, may contain clonal or oligoclonal populations of lymphoid cells, and that these proliferations are part of a continuum from benign lymphoid hyperlasias to malignant lymphomas.
